systems.name: How fast is it going
systems.summary: How fast is a car going when only its position is known? Its speed is the distance covered between two close moments, divided by the time between them. As that time shrinks to zero, the result is the speed at one moment, called the derivative of the position

blocks.label: Speed from two positions
blocks.note: s(t) is the car's distance from the start, in metres, at the time t, in seconds. h is the time between the two readings, set by the page's slider: one reading at t - h/2, one at t + h/2. v is the speed, in m/s. In words: the distance covered between the two readings, divided by the time between them. Example: the braking car at t = 4 s with h = 2 s is at 25.5 m at 3 s and at 37.5 m at 5 s, so v is 12 / 2 = 6 m/s, exactly its true speed

blocks.label: The speed at one moment
blocks.note: The same ratio, with the time h taken closer and closer to zero. lim, the limit, is the value the ratio approaches. The result, written s'(t) and read 's prime of t', is called the derivative of s. On the page, this is the ring landing on the dot

blocks.label: How far off the two-position speed is
blocks.note: The ratio equals the true speed s'(t) plus an error. s⁽³⁾(t), the third derivative, says how fast the acceleration changes. The error grows as the square of h: halving the time between readings divides the error by four. For the steady, speeding-up and braking cars the acceleration never changes, so the third derivative is zero and there is no error at all

dimension.label: The five motions on the page
dimension.note: Steady, speeding up, braking, there and back, stop and go, in that order, with s in metres and t in seconds. The true speeds the page compares against are their derivatives: 4, 0.8t, 10 - t, 6cos(t/2) and 3 + 2.8cos(1.4t)

systems.name: Is it speeding up or slowing down
systems.summary: Is the car speeding up or slowing down? The acceleration is the change in speed per second. It is found from the speed the same way the speed is found from the position, so it is a change of a change, called the second derivative

blocks.label: The second derivative
blocks.note: a(t) is the acceleration at the time t, in metres per second each second. v'(t) is the derivative of the speed v. s''(t), read 's double prime of t', is the derivative of the derivative of the position s. In words: the acceleration is the steepness of the speed curve, and the speed is the steepness of the position curve

blocks.label: From three positions
blocks.note: h is the time between readings, set by the slider. Two speeds h apart, each found from two positions h apart, combine into this one formula: the position after, minus twice the position now, plus the position before, divided by h squared. The page does the two stages separately so both can be seen. Example: for the braking car with h = 1 s the top of the fraction is always -1 m, so a = -1 m/s each second

blocks.label: What the sign says
blocks.tex: a > 0 \Rightarrow v \text{ rising}, \qquad a < 0 \Rightarrow v \text{ falling}
blocks.note: An acceleration above zero means the speed v is rising. Below zero it means the speed is falling. While the braking car still moves forward its speed falls, so the acceleration arrow on the page points backward

dimension.label: At the turning point
dimension.note: t* is the moment the car turns round. There its speed is zero but its acceleration is not: the speed passes through zero without staying there. Example: the braking car at t* = 10 s has speed 0 and acceleration -1 m/s each second

systems.name: Adding it back up
systems.summary: Given only the speed of a car, how far has it gone? The time is cut into short slices, each slice gives speed times time, and the slices are added up. With thinner and thinner slices the sum becomes the integral, which undoes the derivative

blocks.label: One slice
blocks.note: Δt, read 'delta t', is the length of one slice, in seconds. tᵢ is the time at which slice number i starts, and v is the speed, in m/s, read at the middle of the slice, tᵢ + Δt/2. Δsᵢ is the distance covered in that slice: speed times time. Example: 5 m/s for Δt = 2 s gives 10 m

blocks.label: All the slices
blocks.tex: s(T) - s(0) \approx \sum_{i} v\!\left(t_i + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\right)\Delta t \;\longrightarrow\; \int_{0}^{T} v(t)\,dt
blocks.note: s(T) - s(0) is how far the car has moved between the time 0 and the time T. The sign Σ means: add up over all slices i. The sign ∫ from 0 to T, the integral, means the same sum with the slices made as thin as wanted. On the page, the staircase of sums turns into the smooth curve

blocks.label: The error of the midpoint rule
blocks.note: Reading the speed at the middle of each slice is called the midpoint rule. Its error is at most T times Δt squared, divided by 24, times the largest size of v''. v'' is the second derivative of the speed and says how much the speed curve bends. Doubling the number of slices halves Δt, so the error falls by four. When the speed is a straight line in time, v'' is zero and there is no error, so the page opens on a speed that bends

blocks.label: The derivative undone
blocks.note: d/dT means the derivative with respect to T: how fast what follows changes as T changes. In words: the steepness of the added-up distance is the speed that was added up. Adding up a speed and then taking the derivative gives the same speed back

dimension.label: Signed area
dimension.note: When the speed v is below zero the car moves backwards, and each slice's distance Δsᵢ counts as negative. The total then comes back down: it measures how far the car is from the start, not how far it has driven

systems.name: The thing that grows by how much there is
systems.summary: An amount that always grows by a fixed share of itself, like money at interest or a population with room to spread. That one rule gives the exponential curve, a fixed doubling time, and the logarithm as the answer to the question 'when'

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.note: A is the amount, t the time in years, r the yearly rate as a fraction (12 % is 0.12). dA/dt is how fast the amount grows, its derivative. In words: the speed of growth is the rate times the amount. Example: A = 100 and r = 0.12 give a growth of 12 a year. The page's lower chart is dA/dt divided by A, which is always r, so it never moves

blocks.label: The only curve that obeys it
blocks.note: A₀, read 'A nought', is the starting amount. e is a fixed number, about 2.718. In words: the amount is the start times e to the power rate times time. Example: 100 at r = 0.12 after 10 years is 100 times e to the power 1.2, about 332. The number e is the base for which the steepness of the curve equals its height exactly, so the constant in the rule is the rate and nothing else

blocks.label: Doubling time
blocks.note: t₂ is the time the amount takes to double. ln is the natural logarithm, the operation that undoes e to a power; ln 2 is about 0.693. Example: r = 0.12 gives 0.693 / 0.12 = 5.78 years. Every doubling takes the same time, which is why the doubling marks on the page are evenly spaced

blocks.label: When does it reach a target
blocks.note: t* is the time at which the amount reaches the target A*. In words: divide the target by the start, take the natural logarithm, divide by the rate. Example: from 100 to 800 at r = 0.12 takes ln 8 / 0.12 = 17.33 years

dimension.label: Against a straight line
dimension.note: A₀(1 + rt) is growth by the same amount every year, A₀ times r, starting at the same speed as the exponential. It falls behind at once and stays behind. Example: from 100 at r = 0.12, after 20 years the straight line gives 340 and the exponential about 1102

systems.name: Which way is down
systems.summary: A ball on a landscape, knowing only the ground under it. At each step it measures the steepness in each direction, together called the gradient, and steps the opposite way. This is gradient descent

blocks.label: Two slopes, one for each way to move
blocks.tex: \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \approx \frac{h(x+\epsilon, y) - h(x-\epsilon, y)}{2\epsilon}, \qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \approx \frac{h(x, y+\epsilon) - h(x, y-\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}
blocks.note: h(x, y) is the height of the ground at the point (x, y) of the map, x across and y up. ε, read 'epsilon', is a tiny distance. ∂h/∂x, read 'partial h by x', is the steepness when only x changes and y is held still; ∂h/∂y is the same for y. Each is the height a little ahead minus the height a little behind, divided by the distance between them, 2ε

blocks.label: The gradient
blocks.note: ∇h, read 'nabla h' or 'the gradient of h', is the pair of the two steepnesses, drawn as one arrow. It points the steepest way uphill, and its length says how steep. Example: in the round bowl at the point (2, 1) the gradient is (2, 1)

blocks.label: One step
blocks.note: η, read 'eta', is the step size set by the slider. The arrow ← means: replace the left side by the right side. In words: move against the gradient, by the step size times the steepness. Example: from (2, 1) in the round bowl with η = 0.1 the ball moves to (1.8, 0.9). Repeating this step is called gradient descent

blocks.label: When the step is too big
blocks.note: λ_max, read 'lambda max', is the largest curvature of the landscape: how fast the steepness grows in its most sharply bent direction. If the step size η is larger than 2 divided by λ_max, each step lands further from the bottom and the ball runs away. In the narrow valley the curvature is 12 across and 1 along, so a step size above 2/12, about 0.167, makes the ball bounce higher each time

dimension.label: Flat is not bottom
dimension.note: A gradient of zero means flat ground, not the lowest point. In the middle of the saddle the ball stops while the ground falls away in one direction. The four landscapes on the page are a bowl, a narrow valley, a saddle and two hills

systems.name: Draw the line by hand
systems.summary: Dots of two colours, and one straight line to separate them. The line is drawn by hand, then Rosenblatt's perceptron tries, one correction at a time. On the four dots of exclusive or it fails, as Minsky and Papert showed in 1969

blocks.label: A line as three numbers
blocks.note: x and y are a point's coordinates. w₁ and w₂ are called weights and b the bias. The points where this sum is exactly zero form a straight line. The weights set which way the line faces, and the bias how far it is from the centre (0, 0). The page turns the two handles of the hand-drawn line into these three numbers

blocks.label: The unit
blocks.note: ŷ, read 'y hat', is the machine's answer for a dot: 1 when the sum is above zero, 0 otherwise. In words: which side of the line the dot is on. A weighted sum and a hard cut at zero, nothing else. This calculation is called a unit, or an artificial neuron

blocks.label: One correction
blocks.note: y is the dot's right answer, 1 or 0, and ŷ the machine's answer. η is a small step, 0.1 on the page. If the answer is right, y - ŷ is 0 and nothing changes. If it is wrong, y - ŷ is 1 or -1, and the weights and the bias move so that the line turns a little towards the dot. The large ring on the page marks that dot

blocks.label: It stops, if it can
blocks.note: R is the distance of the furthest dot from the centre. γ, read 'gamma', is the gap between the nearest dot and the best separating line. When such a line exists, the number of corrections is at most (R/γ) squared, so the rule always stops. On two clouds of sixty dots the page counts two

blocks.label: And when it cannot
blocks.note: xor, exclusive or, gives 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1. Its four dots sit at the corners of a square, with opposite corners alike. No straight line puts all four on their right sides, so there is always a dot to correct and the rule never stops. Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert, 1969

dimension.label: The count for the hand-drawn line
dimension.note: #{...} means 'the number of dots for which...'. A hand-drawn line does not say which side belongs to which colour, so the page counts the mistakes both ways and keeps the smaller count

systems.name: A small change, and what it does
systems.summary: One weight moved by the same small amount, again and again, on a hard unit and a smooth one that share their numbers. The smooth answer changes a little each time, the hard one stays still or jumps. Learning needs the smooth one, because only its changes show which way to move

blocks.label: The two units on the same three numbers
blocks.tex: \hat{y} = \big[\,w_1 x + w_2 y + b > 0\,\big], \qquad a = \sigma(w_1 x + w_2 y + b)
blocks.note: x and y are the dot's coordinates, w₁ and w₂ the weights and b the bias. The square brackets give 1 when the statement inside is true and 0 when it is false: this is the hard unit's answer ŷ. σ, read 'sigma', is the smooth curve 1 / (1 + e to the power -z), which turns any total z into a number a between 0 and 1. Example: a total of 0 gives 0.5, a total of 2 gives about 0.88

blocks.label: One nudge
blocks.note: ε, read 'epsilon', is the size of one nudge, set by the page's slider. Each step adds ε to the weight w₁ and changes nothing else

blocks.label: What the smooth answer does
blocks.note: Δa is the change in the smooth answer after one nudge. σ'(z) is the steepness of the smooth curve at the dot's total z. In words: the steepness of the curve, times the dot's x, times the nudge. Example: at z = 0 the steepness is 0.25, so with x = 0.4 and ε = 0.01 the answer moves by 0.001. Small, nearly the same every time, and its sign shows the direction to move

blocks.label: What the hard answer does
blocks.note: Δŷ is the change in the hard answer. It can only be 0, 1 or -1: nothing until the total crosses zero, then a jump of one. The hard answer has no steepness anywhere, so it shows no direction

dimension.label: Why learning needs the smooth one
dimension.note: L is the error and a - y the miss between the answer a and the right answer y. ∂L/∂w₁ says how fast the error changes as w₁ changes. It exists only because σ has a steepness σ'. For the hard unit the same expression is zero everywhere and undefined at the jump

systems.name: Inside one unit
systems.summary: One artificial neuron: two weights, a bias and a squash curve. The three numbers are moved by hand while the shading of the plane follows, then the neuron moves them itself, downhill on its error

blocks.label: The unit
blocks.tex: a = g(w_1 x + w_2 y + b)
blocks.note: x and y are a dot's coordinates, w₁ and w₂ the weights, b the bias. g is the squash, a curve chosen with the page's buttons, and a is the answer. In words: multiply, add up, shift, squash. Example: x = 0.6 and y = -0.4 with w₁ = 0.3, w₂ = -0.25 and b = 0.15 give a total of 0.43, and the squash to 0..1 turns it into 0.61

blocks.label: The squashes on offer
blocks.note: σ, read 'sigma', squeezes any total z into the range 0 to 1. tanh squeezes it into -1 to 1. max(0, z) keeps a positive total and cuts a negative one to zero. z alone means no squash. σ is built from the exponential curve e to the power -z

blocks.label: The error, as one number
blocks.note: N is the number of dots and n numbers them. a⁽ⁿ⁾ is the unit's answer for dot n and y⁽ⁿ⁾ its right answer. Σ adds over all dots. In words: the squared misses, added up and divided by twice the number of dots. This error is the height that each run step goes down

blocks.label: One step on three numbers
blocks.tex: w_i \leftarrow w_i - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_n (a - y)\,g'(z)\,x_i
blocks.note: wᵢ stands for any of the three numbers, and xᵢ for what it multiplies: x, y, or 1 for the bias. η is the step size. ∂L/∂wᵢ is how fast the error L changes as wᵢ changes. g'(z) is the steepness of the squash at the total z. In words: move each number against the steepness of the error, as a ball steps downhill, with three directions instead of two. This needs the squash to have a steepness, which the hard 0-or-1 rule does not have

dimension.label: The line is still there
dimension.tex: a = \tfrac{1}{2} \iff w_1 x + w_2 y + b = 0
dimension.note: ⟺ means 'exactly when'. With the squash to 0..1, the answer is one half exactly where the total is zero, and those points form a straight line. The squash adds how sure the unit is, on either side of that line

systems.name: Many units, one answer
systems.summary: Several units side by side, each drawing its own line, and one more that weighs their answers. What each unit alone sees, and the bent boundary made of them

blocks.label: The middle layer
blocks.note: Each middle unit is the last page's unit with its own three numbers. The small tiles are these, one each

blocks.label: The last unit
blocks.note: Weighs the middle answers. Its boundary is where their weighted sum crosses zero, which is no longer a line

blocks.label: How many numbers
blocks.note: With H middle units. The page counts them from the network rather than from this

blocks.label: One middle unit is not enough
blocks.note: A squash of a squash of one line is still one line, moved. Two lines can do exclusive or; a ring needs about three

dimension.label: Starting numbers
dimension.note: Xavier's rule, so the first answers are neither all one half nor all saturated. The slider on the page picks a different draw from the same rule

systems.name: Any curve at all
systems.summary: One input, one row of squashing units and one output, with each unit set to be one step of a staircase that follows a chosen curve. More units, or steeper ones, and it follows as closely as wanted. What a network can draw, before any learning

blocks.label: One hidden unit is one step
blocks.note: The weight into the unit is the steepness s and its bias is minus s times the place c_k. As s grows the squash becomes a sharp step at c_k

blocks.label: The output adds the steps up
blocks.note: The output weight r_k is the rise of step k: the target at the middle of one interval minus the target at the middle of the one before. The bias b is the target on the first interval

blocks.label: How close
blocks.note: The page's worst gap, measured on 401 points of the input

blocks.label: The theorem behind the page
blocks.note: For any continuous f. The universal approximation theorem, shown here by building the network rather than by proof; the same construction goes through in any number of inputs

dimension.label: Numbers in the network
dimension.note: Two per hidden unit on the way in, one each on the way out, and the output bias. The page counts them from the network

systems.name: How it learns, and how fast
systems.summary: Step size, how many dots before each move, and the standard tricks, with finished runs kept on one chart. And the one-shot formula that works only when nothing bends

blocks.label: Plain descent
blocks.note: The ball. One fixed step down the slope, on every number at once

blocks.label: A few dots at a time
blocks.note: The slope estimated from B dots instead of all of them. Cheaper and noisier, which is the jagged curve

blocks.label: Momentum
blocks.note: The ball keeps some of its speed, so it stops bouncing across a narrow valley and rolls along it

blocks.label: Adam
blocks.note: Every number gets its own step size, shrunk where its slope has been steep. Adagrad and RMSProp are the two halves of this

blocks.label: The one-shot answer, when nothing bends
blocks.note: With the squashes removed the network is one straight line and the best one has a formula. The dashed line on the page is it, and it cannot bend

dimension.label: When the run blows up
dimension.note: The step overshoots along the steepest direction of the hill and lands higher each time. The page shows the curve going up rather than down

systems.name: The correction, one dot at a time
systems.summary: One correction in six moments: the dot goes forward, the miss is measured, the blame flows back along the wires, every number moves. Backpropagation, checked by nudging

blocks.label: The miss, and the blame at the output
blocks.note: How much the answer is off, times how much the last squash was moving there. A saturated squash passes almost no blame

blocks.label: The blame flowing back
blocks.note: Each middle unit's share is in proportion to its wire into the output, times its own squash's slope. The chain rule, once per layer

blocks.label: What each weight does with it
blocks.note: The blame on the unit it feeds, times the value that came along it. The halos on the page are these

blocks.label: Checked, not trusted
blocks.note: Every slope also computed by nudging the number by hand. The page reports the worst disagreement, which runs around 1e-7 with tanh in the middle

dimension.label: The cost
dimension.note: Thirteen slopes from one pass back, instead of thirteen separate nudges each needing two forward passes

systems.name: Starting sure and wrong
systems.summary: One unit that starts almost certain of the wrong answer, trained twice with the same descent: on the squared miss and on cross entropy. The first barely moves for a long while. The reason the cost for a yes-or-no answer is chosen the way it is

blocks.label: The unit
blocks.note: One input, one weight, one bias, and the right answer is zero. The start slider sets the first answer a

blocks.label: The squared miss, and the move it asks for
blocks.note: The move carries the slope of the squash, which is at most a quarter and near zero far out on the flat, exactly where a sure and wrong unit sits

blocks.label: Cross entropy, and the move it asks for
blocks.tex: L = -\big[\,y \ln a + (1 - y)\ln(1 - a)\,\big], \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (a - y)\,x
blocks.note: The slope of the squash cancels: the cost's own slope with respect to a is (a - y) over a(1 - a), and the squash's slope is a(1 - a). What is left is the miss

blocks.label: The slope out on the flat
blocks.note: At a first answer of 0.98 this is 0.0196, so the squared miss moves the numbers fifty times less than the miss alone would

dimension.label: Steps to admit the mistake
dimension.note: The page counts the steps each copy takes to come within 0.1 of the right answer, from the same start with the same step size

systems.name: The first layer learns last
systems.summary: Many layers stacked on the ring inside a ring, and the blame measured as it flows back through them. It fades at every squash, so the layer that sees the dots moves least. The vanishing gradient, and the two fixes that are on the page

blocks.label: The blame, one layer back
blocks.note: The correction page's rule, once per layer: multiply by the weights, then by the slope of the squash at each unit

blocks.label: What one layer multiplies by
blocks.note: With small weights and a squash to 0..1, each layer back shrinks the blame by a factor of four or more, and the factors multiply

blocks.label: What the bars measure
blocks.note: The root mean square of the slopes on one layer's weights: how far that layer will move on the next step

blocks.label: The two fixes on the page
blocks.note: A squash whose slope is exactly one wherever it is on, and a start sized so the signal keeps its size through each layer. Skip connections are the third fix and are not on the page

dimension.label: Last over first
dimension.note: The ratio the page reports. Above a hundred the first layer is as good as frozen and learns last, if at all

systems.name: The same job on a picture
systems.summary: One small pattern slid over a drawing, the strongest fits kept, the nearest shape named. A convolution, pooling, and why the shape may move and still be found

blocks.label: One position
blocks.note: The patch under the pattern, times the pattern, added up, cut below zero. The page shows this one position at a time

blocks.label: The whole map
blocks.note: A hundred numbers from nine weights, because the same nine are used everywhere. A unit wired to every pixel would need one weight per pair

blocks.label: Pooling
blocks.note: Keep the largest of each block and forget where inside the block it was. This is what lets the shape move a pixel

blocks.label: The nearest shape
blocks.note: The pooled map against the pooled map of each remembered shape. A trained network would learn this last step too; here it is written out

dimension.label: The patterns on the page
dimension.note: The vertical-edge pattern: large where the left of a patch is brighter than its right. The others are its turn, a blur, a sharpen and a corner

systems.name: The same job on a sequence
systems.summary: Numbers arriving one a step; say the first one at the end. A gated memory cell beside a plain loop, with the gates set by hand so the mechanism is visible

blocks.label: The plain loop
blocks.note: The answer fed back in. Every step overwrites the state, so the first number fades within a few steps

blocks.label: Three gates
blocks.note: Each a small unit looking at the new number and the last output: how much to keep, how much to let in, how much to show

blocks.label: The memory
blocks.note: Kept part plus let-in part. The plus sign is the whole point: added to, not replaced

blocks.label: What is shown
blocks.note: The memory can hold a value without showing it, and show it later

dimension.label: Why the first number survives
dimension.tex: f_t \approx 1,\ i_t \approx 0 \text{ for } t > 1 \Rightarrow c_t \approx c_1
dimension.note: With the gates set to hold, the memory after step one is left alone. Blame flowing back across the plus sign is not shrunk at each step, which is what a plain loop cannot manage

systems.name: The same job on words
systems.summary: Each word decides which words to listen to, and how much. One head of attention, wired by hand so the pattern can be read off

blocks.label: A question, a key and a value for every word
blocks.tex: q_i = W_q x_i, \qquad k_j = W_k x_j, \qquad v_j = W_v x_j
blocks.note: Three projections of the same vector. The vector carries the position as a point on a circle and the word as a few numbers

blocks.label: How much i listens to j
blocks.note: The match between a question and a key, squashed so each row adds to one. The exponential page's curve again

blocks.label: What the word carries out
blocks.note: The values of the words it listened to, weighed as the table shows

blocks.label: May only look back
blocks.note: A model that writes one word at a time has no words ahead of it yet. The dark cells in the table are this

dimension.label: A head that means 'the word before'
dimension.tex: q_i = R(-\theta)\,\mathrm{pos}_i, \qquad k_j = \mathrm{pos}_j \;\Rightarrow\; q_i \cdot k_j \text{ largest at } j = i - 1
dimension.note: Rotate the question's position back one step and it lines up with the key one position earlier. A trained head that does this is doing the same thing with numbers it found itself

definitions.name: The chain rule
definitions.note: The whole of backpropagation is this, applied once per layer from the output backwards, with the intermediate values kept from the forward pass rather than recomputed

definitions.name: The gradient
definitions.note: The derivative of one number with respect to many. It points the steepest way up the surface, which is the only reason walking the other way is the algorithm

definitions.name: The Hessian, and the curvature it carries
definitions.note: The second derivatives. Its largest eigenvalue sets how long a step can be before descent diverges, and its signs say whether a flat point is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle

definitions.name: The finite difference, and its two errors
definitions.note: The definition of a derivative, computed. One error falls as the step shrinks and the other grows, so there is a best step and it is around 1e-4 rather than as small as possible

definitions.name: The variance a layer passes on
definitions.note: Which is why the fan-in appears in every initialisation scheme: the weight variance has to cancel it or the signal grows or shrinks by the same factor at every layer
